vignette:
Daniel is a 45-year-old military medic, a man who has dedicated his life to serving others, often in the most challenging circumstances. He wears his profession like a badge of honor, and yet, beneath that exterior, he carries the weight of trauma that has reshaped his existence. 

It has been nearly two years since the earthquake struck in the region where he was deployed on a humanitarian mission. The night the earth trembled remains etched in his memory with vivid detail - the sound of buildings collapsing, the cries of the wounded, and the feeling of helplessness that washed over him as he navigated the chaos. He remembers the adrenaline coursing through his veins as he rushed to set up triage, his training kicking in instinctively, yet the sound of despair surrounding him was deafening. There was no time to process what was happening; he was fully immersed in his role, focusing on saving lives, unable to consider the toll it was taking on his own psyche.

In the months following the disaster, Daniel heads back to his civilian life, trying to return to normalcy. But the weight of what he witnessed lingers. He finds himself waking up in the middle of the night, drenched in sweat, heart racing, reliving the chaos. The tremors, now mere echoes in his mind, still feel fresh. He often dreams of the children he could not save, their faces haunting him in the dark. 

At work, Daniel tries to maintain his composure, assisting in the emergency room of a local hospital. However, every siren that blares outside sends him spiraling back to that night. He feels a knot in his stomach, his breath quickening as he recalls the screams, the frantic rush of bodies, and the overwhelming sense of loss. He hides his panic behind a stoic facade, pushing through the day while internally grappling with the remnants of his trauma. 

He isolates himself, avoiding gatherings with friends and colleagues. He feels like an outsider, even among those who share his profession. They talk about the trauma they've faced in their own deployments, but Daniel finds it hard to engage. He feels their stories are distant compared to his own, and he fears that if he opens up, he will be overwhelmed by emotions he has kept at bay. Instead, he spends evenings alone, often scrolling through pictures of his late wife, who passed away three years prior to the disaster. He misses her warmth and understanding; she was his anchor in turbulent times. The irony of his work is not lost on him: he saves lives, yet he feels he has lost everything.

As days turn into months, Daniel starts to notice the shifts within him. He becomes irritable, snapping at colleagues and avoiding his close friends. He is plagued by guilt, often wondering if he could have done more during the disaster. His mind races with an unrelenting internal dialogue, questioning his worth and competence. These thoughts are compounded by the loneliness that envelops him. He can't shake the feeling that he is drifting further away from the man he used to be.

One day, while on his way to work, he sees a news report about a recent natural disaster in a different part of the world. Instantly, his palms sweat, and his heart pounds. The memories flood back, overwhelming him with a sense of dread. He pulls the car over, breathing heavily as he fights against the tide of emotions threatening to drown him. It is in these moments that he realizes he cannot keep suppressing what happened. He needs help, but the thought of reaching out terrifies him.

In the therapy sessions, he recounts the events of that fateful night, articulating the grief and guilt that have consumed him. He shares how he struggles with flashbacks and hypervigilance, feeling like he is always waiting for the next disaster to strike. As he begins to articulate his feelings, a flicker of hope ignites within him. Daniel knows the journey to healing will be long and uncertain, but he feels a cautious optimism that perhaps he can learn to navigate his pain and reconnect with the life he once cherished.
